extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, disciplinary counsel, and Board adjudicators handling attorney ethics in PTO interference litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria for evaluating attorney conduct (dishonesty, misrepresentation, prejudice to administration of justice, duties to disclose) in patent interference depositions, filings, and related communications. Focuses on application of Rule 10.23(b)(4)/(b)(5) and related professional responsibility principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of misrepresentation / concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: A misrepresentation includes false assertions by words or any conduct that amounts to a false assertion; concealment or non-disclosure may have the effect of a misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Black's Law Dictionary and Restatement (Second) of Contracts; concealment of a material fact, if there is intent to mislead, may violate disciplinary rules prohibiting dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation (e.g., Attorney Grievance Comm'n v. Floyd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(b)(4) — prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.23(b)(4) forbids conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation by a practitioner in matters before the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule's scope includes misrepresentations through fabricated exhibits and applies regardless of whether the conduct occurred in deposition or trial; no categorical exception exists for using fabricated documents to test witnesses. Case guidance includes Metzger, Thoreen, Friedman, and Statzer finding such conduct improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated document presented as genuine constitutes misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating, presenting, or examining a witness with a fabricated exhibit that suggests it is genuine is a misrepresentation when it conveys an assertion not in accordance with the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of sanctioned conduct where fabricated or false-appearing exhibits were used (e.g., creating GX 2195 to 'give it a flavor of authenticity'); cases where attorneys were held in violation even when the misrepresentation was to witnesses outside a courtroom (Statzer, Blanchard, Hetzel, Smith, Price).

rubrics_metrics.name: No blanket exception for deposition or pre-tribunal use
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact the conduct occurred in a deposition (preliminary discovery) does not place it outside the scope of disciplinary rules prohibiting misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositions used as evidence (e.g., in interferences) are analogous to courtroom testimony and may be subject to the same high standards (Statzer). Arguments that Rule 10.23(b)(4) only applies at trial are rejected where the deposition testimony is evidence before the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible tactics vs misrepresentation (hypotheticals and identifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of fabricated information within a hypothetical question or explicitly identified as fabricated may not constitute misrepresentation because it is not presented as factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kestler reference: fabricated information may be used as 'bait' if precautions (e.g., hypothetical framing) are taken. In Terry, the attorney revealed the counterfeit immediately after questioning; immediate identification or use as a hypothetical mitigates misrepresentation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty-to-disclose prerequisite for omission-based misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: An omission or non-disclosure constitutes fraud/misrepresentation only when accompanied by intent to deceive and where circumstances create both opportunity and a legal duty to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations creating a duty include fiduciary relationships, submissions to a court, responses to discovery requests, or statements under oath. Authorities cited: State ex rel. Nebraska State Bar Ass'n v. Douglas; Tan v. Boyke; The Mississippi Bar v. Land; In re Slattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evasive/equivocal statements vs affirmative misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evasive, non-committal language (e.g., 'as far as I am aware') can be characterized as partial truths or delay tactics but do not automatically constitute dishonest misrepresentation unless there was a duty to disclose and intent to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context matters: emails that are evasive may be permissible absent a legal duty to disclose (informal emails are not equivalent to discovery responses or sworn statements). The board found OED did not establish intent to mislead Chiron's counsel by emails where Respondent used hedging language and no formal disclosure duty existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Rule 10.23 obligations — tribunal/PTO vs opposing counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.23 explicitly covers knowingly giving false or misleading information to a client or to the PTO/its employees, but does not by its terms include giving false information to opposing counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction reflects a lower level of affirmative disclosure obligation to opposing counsel than to clients or tribunals; therefore failing to disclose document origins in an informal email to opposing counsel is not per se a Rule 10.23 violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (Rule 10.23(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner's conduct that is 'prejudicial to the administration of justice'—i.e., hampers the efficient and proper operation of the courts or ancillary systems—is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting fabricated evidence and not informing the Board/opposing counsel can be prejudicial by depriving the opposing side an opportunity to rehabilitate witnesses, causing wasted time and expense (example: Chiron's search costs). Case law (Iowa Supreme Ct. Bd. of Prof'l Ethics & Conduct v. Steffes) and Board findings support this reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened standards for depositions in interference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions in interference proceedings are analogous to cross-examination before a tribunal and may demand an even higher standard of professional conduct due to absence of a presiding judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing Order Section 46 contains detailed deposition conduct guidelines (e.g., do not confer off the record, do not discuss documents privately with witness) and courts have indicated depositions used as evidence should be conducted 'as if before a tribunal' (Statzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm to truth-finding as central evaluative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Misrepresentations that confuse or intimidate witnesses and thereby impair the reliability and probative value of testimony are especially problematic because they obstruct the truth-finding function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert witnesses under stress rely on authenticity of documents; fabricated scientific data presented as genuine can produce confusion beyond normal cross-examination. The wine-label hypotheticals illustrate how label-based misrepresentation undermines expert identification and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation: prompt disclosure and opportunity to rehabilitate
rubrics_metrics.description: Promptly revealing a fabrication to the witness, opposing counsel, or the tribunal (and giving notice) can mitigate damage and reduce or avoid finding an ethical violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terry: attorney revealed exhibit was counterfeit immediately after questioning; that immediate revelation affected the court's ruling. The Board noted that advance notice or immediate disclosure would have allowed remedial procedures (rehabilitation, rulings) to safeguard the proceeding's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading and notice requirements in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints must provide sufficient notice of alleged conduct and the regulatory provisions alleged to be violated; pleadings are to be liberally construed, but new allegations that would prejudice the respondent require notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph constructions that refer broadly to 'conduct arising from creating, using and introducing false evidence' can encompass post-deposition conduct; but allegations of lying to the Board that were not pleaded and not litigated with notice may be excluded to prevent prejudice (citing In re Ruffalo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for certain allegations (clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some allegations of lying or misrepresentation to the Board require proof by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director observed that OED had not established by clear and convincing evidence that Respondent lied or was dishonest to the Board; therefore, the level of proof required is a material consideration when evaluating such claims.
